Case Vignette: "David"

David is a 54-year-old civil servant who has been living with his partner, Margaret, for twelve years. He presents for therapy at the urging of his primary care physician, who has grown concerned about his worsening insomnia and a pattern of missed workdays. David is a tall, soft-spoken man, with a habit of folding his hands neatly in his lap and keeping his gaze low. He speaks with a careful, measured tone, as if he is constantly editing his own thoughts for safety.

The traumatic event occurred two years ago, in the kitchen of their home. David had come home late from a budget meeting at the local council office. Margaret had been drinking. He does not remember what started the argument—only the sudden, shocking sensation of her hand connecting with the side of his head, then the hard edge of the countertop against his ribs as he tried to shield himself. He remembers the sound more than the pain: the clatter of a chair, the sharp crack of his glasses hitting the tile floor, and then the silence. He did not fight back. He never has. Afterward, he cleaned the blood from his lip, put his glasses back on with a crooked frame, and went to sleep in the guest room. He did not call the police. He did not tell anyone.

In the months that followed, David began to change in ways he could not fully articulate. At work, his colleagues noticed he had become jumpy. He flinched when a supervisor clapped him on the shoulder. He stopped attending the monthly office socials, citing fatigue. In truth, the thought of being in a crowded room, surrounded by laughter and sudden movements, made his chest tighten until he felt he could not breathe. He began arriving at the office an hour early, just to ensure he had a desk with his back to the wall. If someone walked up behind him without warning, his heart would pound so violently he could feel it in his throat.

At home, the hypervigilance is constant. David now tracks Margaret’s mood like a weather system. He notes the pitch of her voice when she answers the phone, the speed of her footsteps on the stairs, the way she sets down a glass. He has learned to read the micro-signals that precede an eruption: a certain tightening around her mouth, a shift in her posture. When he senses danger, he becomes still and quiet, a survival strategy that once kept him safe but now defines his existence. He has stopped inviting friends over. He has stopped cooking her favorite meals, because he cannot predict whether she will be pleased or offended.

The nightmares began six months ago. He dreams of the kitchen, but in the dreams, the details are wrong. Sometimes he is younger, a child again, trying to protect his mother from his father’s fists. Sometimes Margaret’s face is replaced by a stranger’s. He wakes drenched in sweat, disoriented, his hands balled into fists under the pillow. He now sleeps in the guest room permanently, telling Margaret it is for his back pain. She has not questioned it.

David avoids any reminder of that night. He cannot watch television shows with domestic arguments. He has stopped buying wine for the house, because the sight of a bottle on the counter brings the memory rushing back with visceral clarity—the smell of her breath, the feel of the linoleum against his cheek. He is ashamed of this avoidance. He is a rational man, he tells me. He knows she is not always dangerous. But knowing does not stop the automatic response, the way his body braces for impact at the sound of a raised voice in a grocery store.

He has not told Margaret he is in therapy. He fears her reaction—not violence, he insists, but a kind of wounded confusion that would make him feel cruel. He has spent his life managing other people’s emotions, and the thought of causing her pain feels unbearable. So he carries the story alone, like a stone in his chest.

At fifty-four, David feels older than his years. He is tired. He is still going to work, still filing reports, still answering emails with professional courtesy. But inside, he is living in a state of constant, low-grade emergency. He does not know how to stop.
